question: According to the final report of the French parliamentary committee of enquiry into the Uber files1, the company allegedly operated unfairly, claiming to be loss-making while keeping fares low thanks to investments from large financial market bodies. This modus operandi raises concerns about fair competition in the transport and digital services sector.

In addition, the investigations reveal that Uber allegedly transferred funds to tax havens and engaged in intensive lobbying to recruit politicians all around the world, with the aim of boosting their own approval ratings and influencing political decisions to its own advantage. Given the above: 1.

What action does the Commission intend to take to investigate Uber’s alleged breaches of commercial rules and assess the impact of these practices on competition in the European transport and digital services market?
How does it intend to ensure that big digital platforms are transparent and comply with commercial rules so as to promote fair competition and protect the interests of users and competing companies?

What measures will it take to prevent big digital platforms transferring funds to tax havens and to ensure that these companies pay taxes in the countries where they operate, in accordance with EU law?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.4.2024) 1. Any alleged breach by a transport services provider of Member States’ national laws in commercial, labour or transport matters falls under the remit of the competent national authorities. At present, there is no formal investigation by the Commission against Uber under EU Competition law.

As part of its general market monitoring, the Commission keeps a watchful eye on the practices of transport services providers in order to detect any potential anticompetitive behaviour. 2. The Commission stays committed to ensuring a competitive level-playing field in the digital sector.

For specifically designated providers of online intermediation services under Regulation (EU) 2022/1925, (‘Digital Markets Act’), the obligations laid out in this Regulation have become applicable on 7 March 2023. And designated providers of intermediary services under Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (‘Digital Services Act’) have to comply with the set of protective rules set out in the Regulation.

Moreover, under Regulation (EU) 2019/1150 (‘Platform-to-Business Regulation’) digital platforms are required to ensure transparency and fair conditions in the relationship with their business users. These regulations are without prejudice to the implementation of EU competition rules (Art. 101 and 102 Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union) and to national competition rules. 3.

In application of the Guidance of the Code of Conduct Group (COCG) on tax defensive measures, Member States are required to apply at least one tax defensive measure of an administrative nature and one of a legislative nature against non-cooperative jurisdictions included in the EU list, from a list of measures1. Work is ongoing within the COCG on further coordination of tax defensive measures.

In addition, the Commission actively supports the work of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)/G20 Inclusive Framework on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) regarding the adoption of a Multilateral Convention to implement the ‘Pillar One’ reform (reallocation of taxing rights to market jurisdictions with respect to a share of the profits of the largest and most profitable multinational enterprises operating in their markets).
The Commission stands ready to consider any legislative proposal to implement Pillar One in the EU as soon as the work at the OECD level is finalised.
1 See Guidance in Annex IV of the COCG report, endorsed by the Council on 5 December 2019
